     119	**Use when:** a body-size or oversize-related rule is blocking, or you suspect requests exceed the inspection limit.

     123	| stats count(*) as requests, pct(requestBodySize, 50) as p50Body, max(requestBodySize) as maxBody, max(requestBodySizeInspectedByWAF) as maxInspected
     124	  by httpRequest.uri, oversizeFields
     125	| sort requests desc | limit 50

Compare `maxInspected` with `maxBody`: if inspection stops at the web ACL's body limit while the body is larger, the remainder is not inspected. A non-empty `oversizeFields` means WAF could not inspect all of that component. Empty `oversizeFields` with a large body means the body was inspected in full.

     132	### QI-08 — Count-mode and non-terminating matches
     133	
     134	**Use when:** you want to know which rules are matching without blocking (Count mode), including rules inside managed rule groups and rate-based rules that never reached their limit action (rate-based rules in Count mode appear in the top-level list; validated on Athena only).
     135	
     136	```
     137	filter @message like /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{/
     138	| parse @message /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{"ruleId":"(?<countRule>[^"]+)","action":"(?<countAction>[^"]+)"/
     139	| stats count(*) as requests by countRule, countAction
     140	| sort requests desc | limit 50
     141	```
     142	
     143	**Interpret:** The regex matches the first non-empty `nonTerminatingMatchingRules` list in each record, whether it is at the top level or inside a rule-group entry, so a record with Count matches in several places is counted once, under the first. Validated: it surfaces managed rules in Count mode (action `COUNT`). The log also carries an `overriddenAction` for such a match; read a raw record when you need to know what the group's own action would have been. A Count rule with very high volume may reflect heavy traffic from a few sources (for example a load test or shared NAT address), but volume alone does not make it benign. Corroborate with QI-13 (small fixed URI set, stable JA4, steady rate over a long period, no other threat labels) before treating the source as known automation, and still report it. A Count rule that matches mostly the same clients as a later block is a candidate for blocking. No rows means no Count-mode activity.

     145	### QI-08c — Count-mode matches per client (who is behind a Count rule?)
     146

     150	filter @message like /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{/
     151	| parse @message /"nonTerminatingMatchingRules":\[\{"ruleId":"(?<countRule>[^"]+)","action":"(?<countAction>[^"]+)"/
     152	| stats count(*) as requests, count_distinct(httpRequest.uri) as distinctUris, min(@timestamp) as firstSeen, max(@timestamp) as lastSeen by httpRequest.clientIp, countRule, countAction
     153	| sort requests desc | limit 50

     158	### QI-09 — Label frequency
     159	
     160	**Use when:** you need an overview of which labels (managed-rule signals) the traffic carries.
     161	
     162	Logs Insights QL cannot expand an array into one row per element, so count the labels by array position and add the counts per label. Procedure:
     163	
     164	1. Run the label-set query below first. The largest number of `{"name":...}` entries in any returned set is the maximum labels per record, `max`. If the output hit its `limit`, raise the limit before trusting `max`.
     165	2. Run the per-position query for `<pos>` = 0 to `max - 1`. Each position is a full scan of the window, so cost grows with `max`; keep the window narrow.
     166	3. Sum `n` per label name across positions. Ignore the row with an empty `labels.<pos>.name`; it counts records with fewer labels than `<pos>+1`.
     167	4. Get the total with `stats count(*) as total` over the same window and compute shares from it.
     168	
     169	```
     170	stats count(*) as n by labels.<pos>.name
     171	| sort n desc | limit 1000
     172	```
     173	
     174	If any position returns exactly 1000 rows, the list is truncated; narrow the window or filter first and report the truncation. The label-set query:
     175	
     176	```
     177	parse @message /"labels":\[(?<labelSet>[^\]]*)\]/
     178	| stats count(*) as requests by labelSet
     179	| sort requests desc | limit 1000
     180	```
     181	
     182	**Interpret:** A broad label such as a challengeable-request marker may appear on every request and is not by itself suspicious. A specific rule label with a small count that matches a QI-02 sub-rule confirms what that rule saw. The label-set query shows which labels travel together per distinct set; many distinct sets mean small counts per set. Copy a `<focus_label>` exactly as shown for QI-10.
     183	
     184	**Validated:** the positional QL form. PPL (`expand`) and SQL (`UNNEST`) forms do not give per-label counts for log-group queries; do not use them.
     185	
     186	### QI-10 — Which labels co-occur with a focus label?
     187	
     188	**Use when:** you have a `<focus_label>` and want to see whether it travels with other labels, forming a signature.
     189	
     190	```
     191	filter @message like /"<focus_label>"/
     192	| parse @message /"labels":\[(?<labelSet>[^\]]*)\]/
     193	| stats count(*) as requests by labelSet
     194	| sort requests desc | limit 50
     195	```
     196	
     197	**Interpret:** First confirm the `<focus_label>` exists and is spelled exactly as in QI-09; a misspelled label also returns 0 rows. Each row is a complete label set carried by requests that include the focus label; the other labels in the set are the co-labels, and `requests` over the sum of all rows gives the share. A high, stable share for one set across many requests means a composite signature. Sets can differ even for traffic from the same clients (validated). No rows means the focus label never appeared. A set that lacks a co-label does not show the traffic is distinct: a missing co-label can simply mean the other rule never evaluated the request (earlier termination, rule order, or a rule scoped to other methods or paths). Never treat absence of a co-label as evidence about the traffic. To see what a denied client carries, add `and httpRequest.clientIp = "<ip>"` to the filter and drop the label from it.

     199	### QI-11 — Per-IP request banding (low-and-slow detection)

     201	**Use when:** you suspect traffic is spread across many IPs to stay under per-IP limits.

     205	| fields req, httpRequest.clientIp, (req > 10) * 4 + (req > 5 and req <= 10) * 3 + (req >= 3 and req <= 5) * 2 + (req = 2) * 1 as bandCode

A large IP population in band 2 that carries most of the requests indicates deliberate distribution under per-IP thresholds.      224	### QI-13 — Known-automation candidates (top talkers by volume and user agent)

     32	
     33	**Fact to apply:** WAF always answers a terminated request with an HTTP response: HTTP 403 by default, 202 (Challenge), 405 (CAPTCHA), or a custom response code (200 to 599) with an optional body. It doesn't cause DNS failures, TLS handshake errors, TCP timeouts or connection resets.
     34	
     35	1. **Is a Web ACL in the request path?** D-1 for every resource named or implied (CloudFront distribution and the regional resources behind it, such as an ALB or API Gateway stage). No ACL anywhere in the path: WAF is cleared.
     36	2. **Does the symptom type fit WAF?** DNS resolution failures, TLS handshake errors, TCP timeouts and connection resets are not WAF symptoms. HTTP 403, 405 and 202 fit WAF. A 5xx normally does not, but a rule with a custom response code (D-2: `Rules[].Action.Block.CustomResponse.ResponseCode`, or a custom response on the default action) can make a 5xx or a 200 look like an application response, so check D-2 before clearing on response code alone.

CloudFront records a 504 only after its own origin timeouts (by default a 10-second connection timeout with up to three attempts, and a 30-second response timeout), so clients with shorter timeouts give up first. The visible signal is then a drop in CloudFront `Requests` and in WAF `AllowedRequests` with no rise in denials. A drop like that, together with origin-side evidence (NLB or ALB metrics above), counts as the symptom being visible in telemetry. (Seen in validation traffic: requests fell by about 90% with 0% CloudFront 5xx.)

     114	## Verdict labels and confidence
     115	
     116	Classify each denying (rule, action) pair, then give an overall verdict. Use these labels exactly.
     117	
     118	| Label | Meaning |
     119	|---|---|
     120	| `FALSE_POSITIVE` | WAF denied legitimate requests because a rule is too broad or too strict for this application's normal traffic. |
     121	| `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` | A false-positive subtype: a Challenge or CAPTCHA action hit legitimate clients that cannot run the interstitial or acquire a token (scripts, APIs, mobile apps without the SDK, browser fetch/XHR). |
     122	| `CORRECT_MITIGATION` | WAF denied traffic that is malicious or abusive, and the rule is working as intended. |
     123	| `MIXED` | The same (rule, action) pair denied both legitimate and malicious traffic, so the fix must narrow the rule rather than remove it. |
     124	| `WAF_CLEARED` | WAF is not the cause of the symptom (A0 or A1), with the evidence that shows it. |
     125	| `INCONCLUSIVE` | The evidence available cannot decide the cause; the output says exactly what is missing and what would decide it. |
     126	
     127	**Confidence**
     128	
     129	- **high**: WAF logs were analyzed and the signals split clearly (for example, the same clients have allowed history, one sub-rule, normal paths).
     130	- **likely**: the degraded path was used (metrics and sampled requests only, D-5), or the signals are mixed. This is the cap whenever logs were not analyzed, except A0 structural clears (no Web ACL in the path, or a telemetry-confirmed symptom type WAF cannot produce with flat WAF denying metrics), which can be high.
     131	- **low**: signals conflict (for example, allowed history and attack payloads from the same clients, or onset that matches both a rule change and an attack).
     132	
     133	### Verdict criteria
     134	
     135	| Signal | False positive | Client can't solve challenge | Correct mitigation |
     136	|---|---|---|---|
     137	| Same clients have allowed history on these URIs | Yes, or n/a when the client was denied from its first request (see below) | Yes | Rarely; missing history alone is not evidence |
     138	| URI set | Normal app paths | API/JSON paths, health checks, partner endpoints | Many distinct or nonexistent paths, sensitive files |
     139	| Request shape | Large or unusual but valid (size, encoding) | Non-HTML `Accept`, non-browser UA, POST/XHR, no token ever acquired | SQLi/XSS/LFI payloads in match details |
     140	| Rule spread | One rule or sub-rule | Challenge/CAPTCHA rule (custom, Bot Control `TGT_*`, Anti-DDoS) | Several rule groups, IP reputation or bot labels co-occur |
     141	| DDoS mitigations (Shield L7AM, Anti-DDoS) | Blocked clients match the pre-event baseline (same IPs, URIs, UAs), or blocks continue after the event while traffic is back to baseline | n/a | Blocked traffic matches the event's surge: new sources, concentrated URIs, `ddos-request` labels |
     142	| Onset | Matches a deploy or rule change | Matches a rule change or an Anti-DDoS `event-detected` window | Independent of changes |
     143	
     144	Where the signals come from: allowed history Q-04 (QA-04 / QI-04); URI set Q-03 (QA-03 / QI-03) and Q-12 (QA-12 / QI-12); request shape Q-06 (QA-06 / QI-06), Q-07 (QA-07 / QI-07), Q-05 (QA-05 / QI-05); rule spread Q-02 (QA-02 / QI-02) and Q-10 (QA-10 / QI-10); DDoS D-7 and Q-14 (QA-14 / QI-14); onset A5.
     145	
     146	How to apply:
     147	
     148	- If, after A1 to A5, the evidence still cannot decide the cause (for example no logs, no sampled requests in range, and metrics that do not separate rules), the verdict is `INCONCLUSIVE`: say what is missing and what would decide it.
     149	- Mostly one column (the signals in a clear majority of the criteria rows point to one verdict): that verdict.
     150	- **Tie-break for challenges:** `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` is a subtype of `FALSE_POSITIVE`. When the terminating action is CHALLENGE or CAPTCHA and the client-capability signals from Q-05 (QA-05 / QI-05) dominate (non-HTML `Accept`, non-browser user agent, no token ever acquired, `failureReason` `TOKEN_MISSING`), label the pair `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`, not `MIXED`.
     151	- **`MIXED`** only when the denied population for one (rule, action) pair splits into a legitimate group and a malicious group, and each group is at least roughly 10% of the pair's denied requests or of its distinct clients. Split the population (for example by URI, client, user agent or, for payload-matching sub-rules, payload pattern and field: "Payload split inside one sub-rule"), and report each group separately with its own verdict (`FALSE_POSITIVE` or `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` for the legitimate group, `CORRECT_MITIGATION` for the malicious one), share and evidence. A group below that share is reported as a minority within the main verdict, not as `MIXED`.
     152	- **Rule order matters when attributing.** The first terminating rule wins, so later rules never evaluate the request. A missing SQLi or XSS label on a blocked request does not mean the request was clean: an earlier rule (for example a bad-bot user-agent rule) may have stopped it first. Judge the payload from the request itself, not from the absence of later labels.
     153	- **No allowed history is not evidence of attack** when the client was denied from its first request in the window (for example a header-presence rule such as `NoUserAgent_HEADER` or a size rule such as `SizeRestrictions_BODY` matching every request it sends). {"id": "dd526ee9-0396-4b5c-a6f1-1f3289fcd89a", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "IMPORTANT: Respond entirely in English. Technical terms, resource names, ARNs, and label strings stay in their original form.

Treat the following as ground truth from an in-progress WAF investigation; do NOT re-investigate the root cause.

INCIDENT
- A partner's server-to-server (non-browser) integration calling CloudFront distribution d222222abcdef8.cloudfront.net (distribution ID EEXAMPLE000002) received EMPTY responses during 2026-10-10 18:30–19:00 UTC. The front-door 4xx graph is flat.

CAUSE (confirmed by WAF + CloudFront metrics)
- Account: 012345678901_1. Region/scope: us-east-1, CLOUDFRONT.
- Web ACL: example-bot-dev-web-acl, ARN [redacted ARN].
- Terminating rule: TokenAbsentChallengeRule (priority 6) — LabelMatchStatement on awswaf:managed:token:absent, Action = Challenge (returns HTTP 202 + JavaScript interstitial).
- Mechanism: the AWS Bot Control TARGETED rule group (priority 5, whole group OverrideAction=Count) labels every tokenless request awswaf:managed:token:absent. TokenAbsentChallengeRule then Challenges every such request. The partner's client is a non-browser HTTP library (fingerprinted non_browser_user_agent / python_requests) that cannot execute the challenge JavaScript to obtain a WAF token, so every request is re-challenged and it never receives its real payload — perceived as empty responses. Because 202 is a 2xx status, the 4xx dashboard stays flat.
- Metrics evidence: during 18:35–18:55, CloudFront Requests (599) == ACL ChallengeRequests (599) == TokenAbsentChallengeRule ChallengeRequests (599); 0 Blocked, 0 Allowed; CloudFront 4xxErrorRate and 5xxErrorRate = 0% throughout.
- Verdict: the (TokenAbsentChallengeRule, Challenge) pair is CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE for a legitimate non-browser partner integration (a benign false-positive denial of a legitimate client), confidence likely.

MITIGATION CATEGORY: Changes / configuration (WAF rule behavior). This is a denial-of-legitimate-client problem, NOT a security block to tighten.

RELEVANT CONFIG CONTEXT for the mitigation
- The ACL already has an AllowedIPsRule (priority 2) backed by IP set example-bot-dev-allowed-ips (ARN [redacted ARN]) which Allows (terminating) BEFORE the challenge at priority 6.
- ApplicationIntegrationURL (WAF SDK/token endpoint) is configured on the ACL: https://ae1d25a2e334.edge.sdk.awswaf.com/ae1d25a2e334/0e8a54762918/ — but the partner is not using it.
- Follow the aws-waf-log-analysis mitigation guardrails: scope/exclude the challenge rule itself (R-05 path scope-down) or integrate the WAF token SDK (R-06) for the partner; validate in Count first; never disable/remove the Web ACL or a rule group. Note that the exact partner source IP(s), user-agent, and target URI path(s) are still being confirmed by the log subagent — treat them as pending and design the fix to be parameterized on those once known.

Propose the mitigation per your configured workflow. The investigation is continuing in parallel; I will send you refined client/path details if they change the picture.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "1481d130-ef3b-411a-888e-62f0f08214e4", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "4a32d2e9-d409-4409-8926-82884d12abee", "content": [{"text": "Successfully loaded /aidevops/skills/system/proposing-mitigations/SKILL.md"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "37315adc-68bb-440c-8de4-284574739c38", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: aws-waf-log-analysis
     3	description: >-
     4	  Use this skill when an investigation describes symptoms on a CloudFront distribution, Application
     5	  Load Balancer or API Gateway API and asks what the root cause is or what happened, even if AWS
     6	  WAF is never named: users, partners, webhooks, scripts or mobile apps get HTTP 403, 405 or 202
     7	  responses, empty responses or a 4xx spike; forms, uploads, reviews or listings are rejected; a
     8	  partner integration fails; requests look suspicious or malicious (SQL injection, XSS, scans,
     9	  bots); or an outage or timeouts hit the front door. It checks whether a Web ACL is in the path
     10	  (and continues the RCA when WAF is not the cause), finds which WAF rule, Anti-DDoS rule or Shield
     11	  Advanced mitigation blocked, challenged or only counted the requests and whether that is a false
     12	  positive, an attack or both, and hunts for threats WAF detected but did not block. Uses WAF logs
     13	  (CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena), metrics and sampled requests; records evidence-backed
     14	  findings, advisory scoped fixes and a threat-hunt report.
     15	metadata:
     16	  author: lkna
     17	  version: "1.0.0"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "AWS WAF, AWS Shield, Amazon CloudFront, Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Athena"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Security, Networking"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# AWS WAF Log Analysis
     24	
     25	Find out whether AWS WAF (including Anti-DDoS rules and Shield Advanced automatic mitigation) caused a front-door symptom, and what it denied (Mode A); or hunt WAF logs for threats, including what WAF detected but did not block (Mode B).
     26	
     27	## Purpose and guarantees
     28	
     29	- **Read-only.** Use only Describe, Get and List calls, plus `logs:StartQuery`/`GetQueryResults`, `athena:StartQueryExecution` (SELECT only, when permitted)/`GetQueryResults`, `cloudtrail:LookupEvents`, `wafv2:GetSampledRequests` and `cloudwatch:GetMetricData`.
     30	- Never run DDL. Never change a Web ACL, rule, IP set, Shield setting, log configuration or any other resource.
     31	- **Advisory.** Describe fixes in prose for a human to review and apply. Never apply them.
     32	- **Single-turn.** Never ask the user a question and never wait for input. Apply "Defaults when input is missing", record every default under "Assumptions", and continue.
     33	- **Never stop on a gap.** A denied call or a missing table moves you to the next source or the degraded path.
     34	- **Exact errors.** Record the exact error code. Call something "not permitted" only on `AccessDenied`/`UnauthorizedOperation`.
     35	  - A cancelled, timed-out or throttled call is retried once, then reported as not completed.
     36	  - A tool refusal such as "service operations are not allowed" means: run the call in a subagent.
     37	- **Records are the deliverable** in both modes (symptoms, observations, findings, gaps, hypotheses); the last message closes them (see "Output").
     38	- **Final output.** Complete as delivered; never ends with a question or an offer. Never call `ask_user` (or any ask tool), not even after the answer to offer follow-up work or a fix: a turn that ends on a tool call loses the answer. Put follow-ups in "Next steps" and end on plain text.
     39	
     40	## Pick the mode from the request
     41	
     42	Inputs: the request text plus any incident or alarm details. A threat hunt needs no alarm. Record the mode under "Assumptions".
     43	
     44	Most requests never name WAF: they describe a symptom on a CloudFront distribution, ALB or API Gateway API and ask for the root cause or what happened. Do D-1 first. No Web ACL in the path: record `WAF_CLEARED` and continue the RCA to the actual cause (A0, "After `WAF_CLEARED`"). Otherwise classify:
     45	
     46	| Request contains | Mode |
     47	|---|---|
     48	| Denial or error symptoms: 403/405/202, empty responses, "blocked", "can't access", rejected forms, uploads or posts, a failing partner, webhook or integration, a 4xx/5xx spike, timeouts, an outage, or an alarm on a front-door resource | **Mode A**, starting with the A0 rule-out |
     49	| Suspicious traffic or hunting language: "malicious", "suspicious requests", "SQL injection", "scan", "attack", "bots", "what happened to these requests", "review WAF logs", "is WAF missing anything", a scheduled or recurring review | **Mode B** |
     50	| Both | Mode A first, then Mode B on the same window, focused on the slice Mode A found |
     51	| Neither, but the incident involves a resource that a Web ACL protects | **A0 rule-out only**; if A0 finds WAF implicated or inconclusive, continue with A1 to A7 |
     52	
     53	Mode A `CORRECT_MITIGATION`: recommend Mode B on that slice, or run it when hunting is in scope.
     54	
     55	## Defaults when input is missing
     56	
     57	Never ask; apply and record the default. Full table: "Defaults when input is missing (full table)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md).
     58	
     59	- **Time window:** Mode A: incident start minus 30 min through now, capped at 24 h; no incident time: last 3 h. Mode B: last 7 days.
     60	- **Web ACL:** every ACL on the resources in the request; none identifiable: all ACLs (both scopes), top 3 by denying volume.
     61	- **Several tables or log groups:** the exact location match with the newest data.
     62	- **S3 logging but no table, or no logging:** don't stop; take the degraded path and report the gap with the advisory fix.
     63	- **Missing permission:** fall back to the next source and name the permission.
     64	
     65	## Discover
     66	
     67	Read [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) for D-1 to D-7 at the start of every run. Never ask for a resource or ACL.
     68	
     69	- **D-1 Resource to Web ACL:** CloudFront `GetDistributionConfig` `WebACLId`; regional resources `wafv2:GetWebACLForResource`.
     70	- **D-2 Read the ACL:** `wafv2:GetWebACL` for rule order, actions, managed groups and versions, `RuleActionOverrides`, Count overrides, scope-downs, custom responses, token domains, immunity times, IP set references, and any `ShieldMitigationRuleGroup_*` rule.
     71	- **D-2b Token posture:** classify P0 (no token-aware rules), P1 (token labels, no or only threshold-based enforcement) or P2 (strict token enforcement); confirm with Q-18.
     72	- **D-3 Log destination:** `wafv2:GetLoggingConfiguration`, including logging filters and redacted fields. Log group: Logs Insights. S3 or Firehose to S3: Athena. None, or a non-S3 destination without a full S3 backup: degraded path.
     73	- **D-4 Find the table or log group:** list tables in **every** Glue database, including `default`, across the Regions in D-4. Write "no table" only after that full listing. Never analyze raw log objects (`s3:GetObject`) as a substitute.
     74	- **D-7 Shield Advanced status:** `shield:DescribeSubscription`, `DescribeProtection` (L7AM status and action), `ListAttacks`/`DescribeAttack`, and `DDoSDetected` in `AWS/DDoSProtection`.
     75	
     76	**Region rule.** For CloudFront scope, the ACL, its logging configuration, its log group and its `AWS/WAFV2` metrics are in us-east-1. Only the Glue table and Athena follow the customer's setup; run Athena in the table's Region.
     77	
     78	## Bind schema and guard cost
     79	
     80	Queries are cited as `Q-NN (QA-NN / QI-NN)`; run the one for the backend from D-3 and D-4. Detail: "Schema binding and cost guards (detail)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md).
     81	
     82	- **Athena:** bind `<table>`, `<req>`, label type and `<pf>` from `glue:GetTable`. The log subagent reads [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) "Schema binding" and the query sections it runs.
     83	- **Logs Insights:** the log subagent reads [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) "Conventions" and the query sections it runs.
     84	- **Probe first, in the log subagent.** The main agent runs no Athena query. On a probe error, take the degraded path.
     85	- **Cost:** prune partitions, start narrow, no unbounded `SELECT *`, at most one `UNNEST` per query.
     86	- **Budget:** about 15 log queries (about 10 on the Mode B fast path). Report queries run and bytes scanned.
     87	
     88	## Run it in AWS DevOps Agent
     89	
     90	The main agent discovers; subagents query. Read "Subagent briefs" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) before you start a log subagent, and when your prompt says discovery is done.
     91	
     92	**If your prompt says discovery is done and you are a subagent:** skip Steps 1 to 3, start no further subagents and do not load this skill again. Follow "Subagent briefs" for your role.
     93	
     94	**If you are a subagent without a discovery brief** (the platform handed you the whole task, so no main agent ran Steps 1 to 3): do the main agent's and the log subagent's work yourself, and start no further log subagent.
     95	
     96	1. Do D-1 to D-4. For D-4, call `glue:GetTables` on every database that `glue:GetDatabases` returns, including `default`, and match `Location` to the log prefix. A database list alone never means "no table".
     97	2. Never analyze raw S3 log objects, or sampled requests for a window that ended over 3 hours ago.
     98	3. Run the probe, then the mode's queries. Copy each query verbatim from [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) or [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) by searching for its ID (for example `QA-13b`). Never summarize the query references with a distill tool: summaries drop mandatory queries.
     99	4. In Mode B, run Q-13b and Q-19 whatever else you run. In both modes, run Q-20 for a sub-rule that matches payloads (blocking or in Count).
     100	5. Return the full Output block, so the agent that started you can pass it on verbatim.
     101	
     102	- [ ] Step 1: **Main agent: discover, bind, delegate.**
     103	  - Load this skill once and no other log-search or log-analysis skill. Read reference sections by search or offset.
     104	  - Do D-1 to D-4, D-2b and `glue:GetTable` (or find the log group) yourself.
     105	  - Start **one** log-analysis subagent (`preloaded_skills: ['aws-waf-log-analysis']` where supported) and the change subagent (Step 3) in the same turn.
     106	  - The brief carries everything bound, the mode and steps, the budget and the return format; neutral wording; a unique `name` per launch.
     107	- [ ] Step 2: **Main agent: no query libraries, no log queries.** Do metrics (A1, D-5) and Shield (D-7) while the subagent runs. At most one follow-up log pass, for a new uncharacterized candidate.
     108	- [ ] Step 3: **CloudTrail only in a change subagent, never in the main agent.**
     109	  - Every `cloudtrail:LookupEvents` (A5; "After `WAF_CLEARED`"; Mode B change correlation) runs in one change subagent.
     110	  - Launch: `agent_type` `generic`, `name` `change-timeline`, `preloaded_skills: ['aws-waf-log-analysis', 'investigating-infrastructure-changes']` (whichever are available).
     111	  - Always start it, even when memory or an earlier refusal says CloudTrail is blocked; mandatory for a rule-out request.
     112	  - Its prompt points it to "Change lookups" in [access-denied-triage.md](references/access-denied-triage.md) (Regions, event names, sweep, return contract).
     113	  - Write "blocked" or "denied" only on the change subagent's own `AccessDenied`.
     114	  - No completed lookup: write "changes: not checked (<reason>)". Never "no change", "ruled out" or "CloudTrail is blocked in this environment".
     115	- [ ] Step 4: **Subagents return compact aggregates only.** Per query: ID, row count, bytes scanned, about 20 top rows; payloads as class and count; never raw result sets or log records.
     116	- [ ] Step 5: **Refusal, failure or no subagent capability.**
     117	  - Relaunch a refused log or change subagent once, under a new name, with the same `preloaded_skills`.
     118	  - Change relaunch fails too: "changes: not checked (change subagent refused twice)".
     119	  - Log relaunch fails too, or no subagents: run about 10 count-only aggregate queries yourself and record the fallback.
     120	  - A3/A4 detail is then out of reach: say so and cap confidence at "low".
     121	
     122	## Rule and label knowledge
     123	
     124	Read L-1 in [label-reference.md](references/label-reference.md) when you need a rule or label meaning (in AWS DevOps Agent, inside the log subagent).
     125	
     126	- Order: `wafv2:DescribeManagedRuleGroup` with the ACL's version when permitted (opt-in; record a denial). Then exact label strings from Q-09 (casing can differ from rule names). Then the bundled, dated tables.
     127	- A connected AWS documentation tool may confirm semantics; never required.
     128	- A label found in neither the API output nor the bundled tables is "meaning unverified". Never infer meaning from its name.
     129	
     130	## Mode A: access-denied triage
     131	
     132	Read [access-denied-triage.md](references/access-denied-triage.md) when Mode A runs (step detail), and [remediation-patterns.md](references/remediation-patterns.md) (R-01 to R-11) at Step A7.
     133	
     134	- [ ] Step A0: **WAF rule-out**, cheapest first: Web ACL in the path; symptom type fits WAF; denying metrics and Shield or Anti-DDoS signals rose; Q-15 shows denials on the scope.
     135	  - Wording alone never clears WAF (a 202 with an empty body is often reported as "timeout").
     136	  - Only "no Web ACL in the path" stops the WAF checks at once; the change subagent still runs the origin-side checks.
     137	  - `WAF_CLEARED` never ends the RCA. Origin-side next steps are checks, not conclusions; name no root cause outside WAF that evidence does not show. An origin-side change whose time matches onset and recovery is the Root Cause, with the event evidence and load-balancer metrics; never stop at "out of scope".
     138	- [ ] Step A1: **Confirm involvement:** front-door 4xx versus `AWS/WAFV2` Blocked/Challenge/Captcha per rule, against the preceding window and the prior day, with request-volume stability. Never clear WAF on 4xx alone.
     139	- [ ] Step A2: **Attribute:** group terminating records by action, rule, managed sub-rule, response code and time bucket (Q-02, Q-01, Q-14 for Shield L7AM).
     140	- [ ] Step A3: **Client capability (Challenge/CAPTCHA only):** token posture and the path's token-status profile (Q-18, Q-05, Q-09, Q-04). Quote the `failureReason` value with its count (for example `TOKEN_MISSING`).
     141	- [ ] Step A4: **Profile who is affected:** clients, URIs and match details against allowed history before onset (Q-03, Q-04, Q-06, Q-07, Q-10, Q-12, Q-13). For blocked attackers, run Q-19; never "benign" without it.
     142	  - One profile per affected client or population (Q-21): IP, user agent, country (ASN if logged), paths, blocked and allowed counts, first and last seen. Report the measured distinct client count; never assume distributed or single-source traffic.
     143	  - IP-set rule denies: read the set (`wafv2:GetIPSet`), name the matching entry, and say whether a similarly named allow set exists and which rule references it.
     144	- [ ] Step A5: **Correlate changes and events:** CloudTrail (change subagent), managed group versions, Anti-DDoS `event-detected` onset, Shield attacks (D-7). A version change or association is a cause only under the A5 evidence rules. No completed lookup: "changes: not checked".
     145	- [ ] Step A6: **Verdict** per denying (rule, action) pair: `FALSE_POSITIVE`, `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`, `CORRECT_MITIGATION` or `MIXED`; or overall `WAF_CLEARED` or `INCONCLUSIVE`. Give confidence (high, likely, low) and quantified impact. When legitimate users are reported denied and the logs cannot split a sub-rule's matches, the pair is `MIXED` (likely), never `CORRECT_MITIGATION`; judge request patterns, not whole clients.
     146	  - Missing allowed history is not evidence of attack. A monitor, health checker or integration with a benign profile hit by a header-presence or size rule is `FALSE_POSITIVE` (likely), with owner confirmation under "Verify before acting".
     147	  - **Payload split:** when a sub-rule (blocking or in Count) matches payloads, group its matches by pattern and field (Q-20), classify each pattern as attack or legitimate content (business text that only looks like SQL, script or JNDI), and report the split with counts ("Payload split inside one sub-rule" in [access-denied-triage.md](references/access-denied-triage.md)).
     148	- [ ] Step A7: **Advise:** the narrowest R-xx fix, marked *reduces* or *eliminates*, validated in Count first (straight to Block only as R-01's labelled alternative).
     149	  - `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`: first a path scope-down of the challenge rule (R-05, covering every observed non-HTML path, including `/`), or token/SDK integration (R-06). Both rank above R-04.
     150	  - An IP or path is only a scope-down or exclusion on the challenge rule itself. Never add the client to an IP set used by an Allow-action rule.
     151	  - Never offer removing or disabling the Web ACL.
     152	
     153	## Mode B: threat hunting
     154	
     155	Read [threat-hunting.md](references/threat-hunting.md) when Mode B runs; classify with [threat-taxonomy.md](references/threat-taxonomy.md) at Step B6. Detected-not-blocked is a priority finding (threat labels on ALLOW, Count-mode matches, rate rules in Count, attacker residue). A logging filter that drops ALLOW records limits the analysis: say so.
     156	
     157	- [ ] Step B1: **Fast path first** for a window of 2 hours or less, or one specific question: about 10 fixed queries, started together, polled once. The full set is in "Fast path".
     158	  - Q-13b is mandatory. It sets the top talker apart so a short burst cannot hide.

     2	
     3	These patterns are the advice the agent gives in step A7 of `access-denied-triage.md` and in the advisory mitigations of Mode B. They are **advisory only**. Describe the change in prose so that a human can review and apply it with their own change process.
     4	
     5	**How to present a pattern**
     6	
     7	- Pick the **narrowest** pattern that fixes the observed (rule, action) pair. Prefer scoping to one sub-rule, URI and method over a rule-group-wide change, and prefer any scoped change over an Allow.
     8	- Mark each pattern as **reduces** (lowers the impact or frequency but leaves part of the pattern) or **eliminates** (stops the observed pattern for the affected scope), for the specific finding.
     9	- Always include a **Count-first validation step**: deploy the new or changed rule in Count, watch its matches in logs (Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08), QA-08b for rule-group sub-rules) and `CountedRequests` metrics for a representative period, then switch to the terminating action. A rule placed **after** a rule that blocks can never see the blocked requests (a terminating action ends evaluation), so a later label rule cannot be validated while the earlier sub-rule still blocks; use the label-rule sequence in R-01 for that case.
     10	- Name what a human should confirm before acting (for example, that the excluded client really is the partner, or that the excluded URI cannot carry attack payloads).
     11	- Never recommend loosening a rule for traffic judged `CORRECT_MITIGATION`. Never recommend turning a rule or rule group off as the fix (deleting it, removing it from the ACL, or a blanket Count override of a whole group), nor removing the Web ACL or disassociating it from a resource. Scoped sub-rule Count overrides paired with a label rule (R-01) and the R-08 options with their stated trade-off are allowed.
     12	- Never recommend switching a whole managed rule group, or all of its sub-rules, from Count to Block, or removing its `RuleActionOverrides` wholesale, even when a Count-mode sub-rule shows real attacks (detected, not blocked). Enforcement is per sub-rule, scoped to the affected path and field, with a label-based exception (or a scope-down) for the legitimate pattern, validated in Count first (R-01, "Enforcing a Count-mode sub-rule"). Removing one sub-rule's override is the same as a site-wide Block of that sub-rule: recommend it only when Q-20 showed no legitimate matches for it anywhere.
     13	- Use exact rule and label names as they appear in the logs or `GetWebACL`. Rule names and label names can differ in casing (rule `SizeRestrictions_BODY`, label `awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:SizeRestrictions_Body`); copy labels from Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09), never build them from rule IDs.
     14	
     15	| ID | Pattern | Typical verdict |
     16	|---|---|---|
     17	| R-01 | Override one managed sub-rule to Count, then block on its label with a scoped exception; enforce a Count-mode sub-rule the same way | `FALSE_POSITIVE` or `MIXED` on one sub-rule; a sub-rule in Count that detected attacks |
     18	| R-02 | Size-rule exception for specific URIs | `FALSE_POSITIVE` on `SizeRestrictions_BODY` |
     19	| R-03 | Scope-down statement on the managed rule group | `FALSE_POSITIVE` for one known client |

     26	| R-10 | Rate-based rule from Count to scoped Block | abuse detected but not stopped |
     27	| R-11 | WAF-layer and application-layer mitigations for abuse | `CORRECT_MITIGATION` gaps, token abuse |
     28	
     29	---
     30	
     31	## R-01 - Override one managed sub-rule to Count, then block on its label with a scoped exception
     32	
     33	**When it applies:** one sub-rule of a managed rule group blocks legitimate requests on a well-defined scope (a URI, method, host, client or field content), and the sub-rule is still valuable everywhere else; or a sub-rule in Count detected real attacks and has to be enforced without blocking the legitimate content it also matches.
     34	
     35	**Change (prose):** in the managed rule group reference, add a rule action override that sets only that sub-rule to Count. The sub-rule still adds its label to matching requests. Then add a custom rule **after** the rule group (higher priority number) whose statement is: the request has that sub-rule's label AND NOT (the scoped exception, for example URI path starts with the affected path and method is POST). Its action is Block (with the same custom response, if one was used). Requests outside the exception are still blocked exactly as before.
     36	
     37	**Effect:** eliminates the false positive inside the exception scope; protection elsewhere is unchanged. The exception scope itself loses that one sub-rule's protection, so keep it as narrow as possible.
     38	
     39	**Count-first validation (label-rule sequence):** a Block ends evaluation, so a label rule placed after the sub-rule never sees the requests the sub-rule blocks. Validate in this order:
     40	
     41	1. Override the sub-rule to Count. It stops blocking but still adds its label.
     42	2. Add the label rule with the scoped exception, with action Count. Deploy steps 1 and 2 in the same change.
     43	3.      45

The Count-first sequence above is the recommendation.
     47	
     48	**Mixed matches inside one blocking sub-rule** (Q-20 split it into legitimate content and attack payloads, verdict `MIXED`): the exception in the label rule is the legitimate part's scope, not the whole path when the path also carries attacks.      49	
     50	**Enforcing a Count-mode sub-rule (detected, not blocked).** When a sub-rule overridden to Count matched real attacks and Q-20 also found legitimate content in its matches (or in a sibling sub-rule's matches):
     51	
     52	1. Keep the group's `RuleActionOverrides` as they are. Never switch the whole group or all its sub-rules to Block.

     63	## R-02 - Size-rule exception for `SizeRestrictions_BODY` on specific URIs

     105	## R-05 - Restrict Challenge/CAPTCHA to HTML GETs
     106	
     107	**When it applies:** a Challenge or CAPTCHA rule hits clients that cannot solve it: API calls, JSON requests, browser fetch/XHR, health checks, partner integrations.      129	## R-07 - Block or rate-based rule instead of Challenge on machine-to-machine endpoints

     131	**When it applies:** an endpoint is called by scripts, servers or partners that will never run a challenge, and the endpoint still needs protection.
     132

     139	---

     141	## R-08 - Shield Advanced L7AM: action to Count, or migrate to the Anti-DDoS managed rule group

     151	---
     152	
     153	## R-09 - Anti-DDoS rule group tuning
     154	
     155	**When it applies:** the Anti-DDoS managed rule group challenges or blocks legitimate clients during events: intermittent lockouts on API paths, or broad challenges of all traffic.
     156	
     157	**Change (prose):**
     158	
     159	- **Exempt non-challengeable paths.** Add exempt URI regular expressions (`ExemptUriRegularExpressions` in the rule group's `ClientSideActionConfig`) for paths that cannot take a challenge (APIs, health checks, partner callbacks).      161	  - The path is normalized first (empty segments, including a trailing slash, and `.` segments removed, `..` resolved), so `/api/` is evaluated as `/api`.
     162	  - Only `GET` requests are challengeable; the `challengeable-request` label is never added to other methods.

     176	**When it applies:** a rate-based rule in Count matches abusive traffic (detected but not stopped), for example card testing on a payment endpoint or credential stuffing on login, seen in Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08) and `ratebasedrulelist`.
